question: Which of these is one of the fundamental principles of British life?
options: Democracy
Rule by a single royal family
One compulsory state religion
Control of the country by the armed forces
explanation: Democracy is one of the five fundamental principles of British life, alongside the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance and participation in community life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are fundamental principles of British life?
options: The rule of law
Individual liberty
Loyalty to a particular political party
Compulsory membership of a trade union
explanation: The rule of law and individual liberty are both fundamental principles of British life. Party loyalty and union membership are personal choices, not principles of British life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is a fundamental principle of British life."
options: True
False
explanation: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs is one of the five fundamental principles of British life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: Participation in community life is one of the fundamental principles of British life.
The fundamental principles of British life apply only to people born in the UK.
The fundamental principles of British life are set out in a new law passed every year.
The fundamental principles of British life are decided at each general election.
explanation: Participation in community life is one of the five fundamental principles of British life; the others are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and tolerance.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What should you take with you when you attend the Life in the UK test centre?
options: The same photo ID you used to book the test
A written reference from your employer
A pre-written essay about British history
Your own set of questions to submit
explanation: Candidates must bring the same photo ID they used when booking the test. (The printed handbook also mentioned proof of address.)
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of the following is true about extremism in British society?
options: British society has no place for extremism or intolerance.
Extremism is allowed as long as those involved stay peaceful.
Only people who are not citizens are protected from extremism.
Extremism is tolerated in private but banned in public.
explanation: British society has no place for extremism or intolerance; these are seen as incompatible with the fundamental values of British life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these is a freedom offered to people in the UK?
options: Freedom of belief and religion
Freedom from paying any kind of tax
The right to ignore laws that you dislike
The right to a state-provided home for life
explanation: Freedom of belief and religion is one of the freedoms the UK offers, along with freedom of speech and freedom from unfair discrimination.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are rights or freedoms in the UK?
options: Freedom from unfair discrimination
A right to a fair trial
A right to free housing for life
A right to avoid ever serving on a jury
explanation: Freedom from unfair discrimination and the right to a fair trial are both protected in the UK. Free housing for life and permanent exemption from jury service are not rights.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which right allows people in the UK to help choose who governs them?
options: The right to join in the election of a government
The right to a fair trial
Freedom of belief and religion
Freedom from unfair discrimination
explanation: The right to join in the election of a government allows people to take part in choosing who governs the country.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "In the UK, freedom of speech allows people to express their own views openly."
options: True
False
explanation: Freedom of speech is a freedom the UK offers, so people may express their own views openly.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these is a responsibility of everyone living in the UK?
options: Respecting and obeying the law
Joining a political party
Attending a place of worship each week
Volunteering for the armed forces
explanation: Respecting and obeying the law is one of the responsibilities of people living in the UK.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which responsibility relates to the place where you live?
options: Looking after the area in which you live and the environment
Paying your neighbours' household bills
Attending every meeting of the local council
Joining the local police force
explanation: Residents are expected to look after the area in which they live and the environment.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "People living in the UK are expected to treat others with fairness."
options: True
False
explanation: Treating others with fairness is one of the responsibilities of residents of the UK.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these is a responsibility towards other people?
options: Respecting the rights of others, including their right to their own opinions
Telling your neighbours how they should vote
Reporting neighbours who disagree with you
Choosing which religion your friends should follow
explanation: Residents should respect the rights of others, including their right to hold their own opinions.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: Looking after yourself and your family is a responsibility of people living in the UK.
People living in the UK have no duty to look after their own family.
Only full citizens, and not other residents, are expected to obey the law.
These responsibilities apply only to people over the age of 65.
explanation: Looking after yourself and your family is one of the responsibilities expected of people living in the UK.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: In a democracy, how is the government chosen?
options: By the people through elections
By the monarch acting alone
By senior judges in the courts
By the leaders of the armed forces
explanation: In a democracy the government is chosen by the people through elections.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these best describes democracy as a British value?
options: Decisions are made by representatives whom the people elect.
All decisions are made by one ruling family.
Laws are made only by unelected officials.
Voting is open only to public officials.
explanation: Under democracy, decisions are made by elected representatives chosen by the people.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are features of a democracy?
options: Regular elections in which people can vote
Government by representatives who are accountable to the people
Rule by a monarch who cannot be removed
Decisions made only by the police
explanation: Regular elections and representatives who are accountable to the people are features of a democracy.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "In the UK, people can help choose their government by voting in elections."
options: True
False
explanation: People in the UK take part in choosing their government by voting in elections, which reflects the value of democracy.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What does the rule of law mean?
options: Everyone, including the government, must obey the law.
Only citizens, and not residents, must obey the law.
Judges are allowed to act above the law.
The law applies only inside court buildings.
explanation: The rule of law means that everyone, including the government, must obey the law.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which principle means that no one, however powerful, is above the law?
options: The rule of law
Individual liberty
Tolerance
Participation in community life
explanation: The rule of law holds that no one is above the law, regardless of their position or power.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: A government minister breaks the law. According to the rule of law, what should happen?
options: They should be dealt with by the law in the same way as anyone else.
They should be excused because of their position.
Only Parliament may decide whether the law applies to them.
The monarch alone decides whether they are prosecuted.
explanation: Under the rule of law, everyone is subject to the same laws, so a minister who breaks the law is treated like anyone else.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: The rule of law means that laws apply equally to everyone in society.
The rule of law applies only to people who are not citizens.
The rule of law allows officials to act outside the law.
The rule of law applies only to written contracts.
explanation: The rule of law means that the law applies equally to everyone in society.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What does individual liberty mean?
options: People are free to live their lives and make their own choices within the law.
People may do whatever they wish, even when it harms others.
The state decides which career each person must follow.
Only wealthy people have personal freedom.
explanation: Individual liberty means people are free to live their lives and make their own choices, within the law.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these is an example of individual liberty in the UK?
options: Being free to follow your own religion, or none at all
Being required to join a state-approved religion
Being told by the government which job to take
Being prevented from moving to another town
explanation: Individual liberty includes the freedom to follow your own religion or to have no religion.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are protected by the principle of individual liberty?
options: The freedom to hold your own opinions
The freedom to practise the religion of your choice
The freedom to break the law without consequence
The freedom to ignore other people's rights
explanation: Individual liberty protects freedoms such as holding your own opinions and practising the religion of your choice; it does not allow breaking the law or ignoring others' rights.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which value means accepting people who have different faiths and beliefs?
options: Tolerance
The rule of law
Individual liberty
Democracy
explanation: Tolerance means accepting and respecting people with different faiths and beliefs.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these best describes tolerance in British life?
options: People of different faiths and beliefs are treated with respect.
Everyone is expected to follow the same religion.
Only one set of beliefs may be discussed in public.
People may be punished for holding unusual beliefs.
explanation: Tolerance means that people of different faiths and beliefs are treated with respect in British life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "In the UK, people are free to follow the religion of their choice, or to have no religion."
options: True
False
explanation: Freedom of belief and religion means people in the UK may follow the religion of their choice, or none at all.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What does participation in community life involve?
options: Taking an active part in the life of your local area
Avoiding all contact with your neighbours
Paying a monthly fee to the local council
Serving a set number of years in the armed forces
explanation: Participation in community life means taking an active part in the life of your local area.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these is an example of participating in community life?
options: Volunteering to help with local activities
Never leaving your own home
Refusing to meet other residents
Ignoring problems in your neighbourhood
explanation: Volunteering and helping with local activities are examples of taking part in community life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are ways of participating in community life?
options: Volunteering for a local charity
Helping with a neighbourhood clean-up
Refusing to help your neighbours
Avoiding all community events
explanation: Volunteering for a charity and helping with a neighbourhood clean-up are ways of participating in community life.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens make which of these promises?
options: To show loyalty to the UK and respect its rights and freedoms
To follow every instruction given by their local council
To give up any other nationality they already hold
To serve in the armed forces if they are asked to
explanation: The citizenship pledge includes a promise to give loyalty to the UK and to respect its rights and freedoms.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Besides making the pledge, what do new citizens do at a citizenship ceremony?
options: Swear an oath or make an affirmation of allegiance to the monarch
Sign an employment contract with the government
Vote in their first general election
Hand in any other passports they hold
explanation: At a citizenship ceremony new citizens swear an oath, or make an affirmation, of allegiance to the monarch.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "The citizenship pledge includes a promise to uphold the UK's democratic values."
options: True
False
explanation: The citizenship pledge includes a promise to uphold the UK's democratic values, as well as loyalty and respect for its rights and freedoms.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What does the citizenship pledge say about the law?
options: Citizens will faithfully observe the laws of the United Kingdom.
Citizens may choose which laws they wish to follow.
Citizens are excused from minor laws.
Citizens will help to write new laws.
explanation: In the pledge, new citizens promise to observe the laws of the United Kingdom faithfully.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: To settle in the UK, what level of English are applicants usually expected to show?
options: Speaking and listening at B1 level (ESOL Entry Level 3)
The ability to read ancient Latin
Writing skills at university degree level
Fluency in a second European language
explanation: Applicants normally have to show speaking and listening skills in English at B1 level, which is ESOL Entry Level 3.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which combination is normally required to become a permanent resident or citizen?
options: Passing the Life in the UK test and showing English speaking and listening skills
Passing a driving test and owning property in the UK
Holding a UK university degree and having a job offer
Joining a political party and a trade union
explanation: To become a permanent resident or citizen, applicants normally pass the Life in the UK test and show English speaking and listening skills.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Besides passing the Life in the UK test, what must an applicant usually demonstrate?
options: Speaking and listening skills in English at B1 level
A pass in a British history A-level
Membership of a local charity
Ownership of a home in the UK
explanation: As well as passing the Life in the UK test, applicants normally show speaking and listening skills in English at B1 level.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which TWO of the following are required to become a permanent resident or citizen of the UK?
options: Passing the Life in the UK test
Showing English speaking and listening skills at B1 level
Buying a property in the UK
Living in the UK for exactly one year
explanation: Applicants normally pass the Life in the UK test and show English speaking and listening skills at B1 level. Buying property and a fixed one-year residence are not requirements.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Is this statement true? "People who wish to settle in the UK must show that they have a good understanding of life in the UK."
options: True
False
explanation: Applicants must show they have a good understanding of life in the UK, which is tested by the Life in the UK test.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test?
explanation: The Life in the UK test contains 24 questions.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: The Life in the UK test is based on which official handbook?
options: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents
The British Citizenship Handbook
A Short History of Britain
The New Resident's Guide
explanation: The test is based on the official handbook "Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents".
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: What is the pass mark for the Life in the UK test?
options: 18 out of 24
12 out of 24
24 out of 24
15 out of 24
explanation: The pass mark is 18 out of 24, which is 75 per cent.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts

question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: The Life in the UK test is booked online at gov.uk and taken at an approved test centre.
The test can be taken at any post office without booking in advance.
The test is taken at home using the candidate's own computer.
The test must be taken before you arrive in the UK.
explanation: The Life in the UK test is booked online at gov.uk and taken at an approved test centre.
source: Original practice question based on public handbook facts
